title: Laws of Robotics and Party Rights

jokes.text: 'Which always confuses me, because black means bad... when it's a cat or a banana or a shirt that makes you think you've lost more weight than you have.'
jokes.setup: Jeff starts what sounds like a racial observation about 'in the black' meaning bad
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a completely innocuous list of things where black is actually negative (cat, banana, slimming shirt), defusing the tension with absurd specificity
jokes.explanation: Smart misdirection: the setup mimics an accidental racial gaffe, then the punchline reveals Jeff was just confused about idioms. The slimming shirt detail is an oddly specific and funny kicker. Works because it subverts the expectation of awkwardness with mundane specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to get this school back in the black.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: But Dean, I'm not a color. I'm a person.

jokes.text: 'Did someone use the word "black," and now you want me to give you the all clear? Please tell me that won't be my role in this group.'
jokes.setup: Elroy sees the group looking at him nervously after the 'black' comment
jokes.punchline: He calls out the dynamic directly — that the group wants him to racially sanction things — and refuses the role with dignified exasperation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. Elroy's new-character status makes this especially resonant — the show is literally commenting on how diverse hires get tokenized. 'Please tell me that won't be my role in this group' is a genuinely funny, earned, and socially aware line. Character-specific in a way that couldn't be assigned to anyone else, and it's both the punchline and the thesis statement of the opening scene.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Black licorice? Disgusting. Black olives? No thank you. Blackmail? A crime. See, black means bad.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Black death? Killed millions. Blackheart? A villain. Blacklist? You don't want to be on it.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Black lung disease? Terrible. Black market? Illegal. And black belt? Well, that's just what I need to lose ten pounds.

jokes.text: 'I have a brain the size of Jupiter. I'm nobody's fourth Ghostbuster.'
jokes.setup: Elroy is asserting his intellectual self-worth after being treated as a racial prop
jokes.punchline: The 'fourth Ghostbuster' metaphor — the token addition to a team — is specific, funny, and self-aware
jokes.explanation: The 'fourth Ghostbuster' is a culturally loaded reference — Ernie Hudson's Winston was famously underwritten — deployed here with precision. Pairs perfectly with the previous joke. 'Brain the size of Jupiter' is a great boast that doubles as character introduction.

jokes.text: Jeff's increasingly stumbling attempt to explain the group's past diversity issues: 'before you got here, they had two... No! They had to... often... step back and remind themselves that they weren't one collective ray of light.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to reassure Elroy that the group isn't racist
jokes.punchline: He digs himself deeper with every sentence, the corrections themselves revealing the problem
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the structure of the backpedal — each correction implies something worse than what preceded it. 'Two— No! They had to— often—' reads like a man repeatedly stepping on the same rake. The final line 'one collective ray of light' (meaning they were all white) is surprisingly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: No. I'm not gonna be the guy who gives racial all-clear approval to everything you do. I'm a spaceman. I come from the future. I'm here to teach you about friendship and the cosmos.

jokes.text: 'Is this a cult? Are you gonna eat me?'
jokes.setup: Jeff's rambling about the group being a 'ray of light' has gotten progressively weirder
jokes.punchline: Elroy's paranoid response escalates to cannibalism fear — a deliberately outsized reaction that also reflects legitimate suspicion of this bizarre group
jokes.explanation: Very economical — two short questions that land a good laugh. The cannibalism escalation is funny precisely because it's the logical extreme of cult suspicion. Good character introduction for Elroy as sharp and unimpressed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We don't think in racial terms here. We're a group that transcends race.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're colorblind.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm glad you said that, because I was worried about being the only black person here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're not. We have two Hispanics, an Asian, and a lesbian.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not a lesbian, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: 'No. We're fine. I lived in New York.' — Jeff's non-sequitur reassurance
jokes.setup: Elroy asks if they're a cult that will eat him
jokes.punchline: 'I lived in New York' is offered as though it's self-evidently a credential against being a cannibal cult, with no logical connection explained
jokes.explanation: Classic Community non-sequitur logic — the joke is that Jeff presents 'I lived in New York' as settling the matter. It implies worldliness as a defense against cult membership, which is completely illogical and therefore funny. Very economical.

jokes.text: Nice grammar.
jokes.setup: Britta has just used a correct but awkward double negative ('not not a rager')
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dry compliment acknowledges the linguistic feat while undercutting it — a two-word joke that lands clean
jokes.explanation: Two-word callback that is funnier than it has any right to be. Perfect economy. Jeff's sardonic acknowledgment of Britta's verbal achievement is the ideal reaction-beat line.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm starting to think this group might be a cult.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: First you're all standing around like a collective ray of light, and next thing I know, you're eating people.

jokes.text: 'Eight guests? That's not "not a rager." That's not a party.'
jokes.setup: Annie explains the apartment has a rule against more than eight guests
jokes.punchline: Britta's double-negative construction ('not "not a rager"') accidentally makes a sharp logical point while revealing her anarchist personality
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — the double-negative logic is mildly funny and the follow-up 'Nice grammar' from Annie is a good button. Not exceptional but does character work for Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wow, Britta. A double negative. So that means it IS a rager. Congratulations on accidentally telling the truth.

jokes.text: 'You have a rule against parties, which I'm sure is a world record for uptightness, so let's celebrate that. I'll bring the booze and more than eight guests.'
jokes.setup: Annie defends the eight-guest rule
jokes.punchline: Britta sarcastically suggests celebrating their uptightness with a party — using their own rule-breaking as the joke
jokes.explanation: Good Britta character work — her anarchist logic turns their rule against them. Functional and in-character but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We should celebrate being uptight. That would be a party!

jokes.text: 'Britta, you just moved in. You don't even have a real bedroom. You're a coucher.' / 'She sleeps... on the couch! She's a coucher!'
jokes.setup: Britta tries to exercise apartment authority despite being the newest and lowest-status resident
jokes.punchline: 'Coucher' — a made-up word combining 'couch' and the -er suffix of 'moocher' — becomes a mockingly official label, then the group piles on gleefully
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best running gag launchers. 'Coucher' is a great coinage — it sounds official while being ridiculous, and the immediate group pile-on (complete with the rhythm of 'She sleeps... on the couch! She's a coucher!') turns a single insult into a chant. High quotability and sets up callbacks throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So you're basically a couch sleeper.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Why does that sound like I'm a subcategory of human?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because you are.

jokes.text: 'There's no government to overthrow here.' / 'I'm not overthrowing...' / 'You're overthrowing if I say so.'
jokes.setup: Britta is accused of acting like she's staging a coup in the apartment
jokes.punchline: Annie's 'You're overthrowing if I say so' is itself an authoritarian declaration — she becomes what she's accusing Britta of
jokes.explanation: Smart joke structure: Annie accuses Britta of overthrowing her authority, then exercises that authority in a comically dictatorial way. The irony is self-aware and sharp — 'Nice irony' even lampshades it. Good character comedy for both.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A coucher! You know, someone who coughs and coughs but won't go to a doctor. You just keep coughing on everyone like some kind of coucher!

jokes.text: 'I resent the idea that this would alarm me.'
jokes.setup: Dean says 'Don't be alarmed' as he rolls in on a robot
jokes.punchline: Elroy refuses the premise — he's too cool to be alarmed — which is itself a funny deflation of the moment's intended drama
jokes.explanation: Good Elroy character work — he consistently deflates the group's reactions with dignity. 'I resent the idea' is a funny, specific word choice for mild indignation.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not going to follow some arbitrary rules just because they're written down. Rules are meant to be questioned!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, it's about keeping the apartment clean and respecting everyone's space.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's exactly what they want you to think. This is about control, man. I'm fighting for our freedom.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're fighting to leave your dishes in the sink.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's a metaphor!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's really not.

jokes.text: 'That's the black guy in every sci-fi movie. I'll allow it.'
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Elroy himself, or a reaction to a character framing robots as threatening) says the alarmed-Black-man-at-robots trope applies here
jokes.punchline: Elroy self-awards permission to have that reaction, which is both self-aware and funny — he's acknowledging the cliché and opting into it deliberately
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Elroy calls out a film trope (the skeptical Black character in sci-fi who warns about technology), then grants himself permission to inhabit it. 'I'll allow it' is perfect — legalistic, self-aware, funny. This is the payoff of his new-character arc in this scene: he's not going to be the racial prop, but he WILL consciously choose his own tropes. Genuinely original and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're overthrowing if I say so!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's literally the definition of authoritarianism.

jokes.text: 'They can't rape you because their genitals will be hundreds of miles away.'
jokes.setup: Someone panics that robot-prisoners will rape people
jokes.punchline: Frankie calmly points out the physical impossibility — genitals are geographically separated from the robots — delivered with complete clinical composure
jokes.explanation: Possibly the episode's single funniest line. The genius is Frankie's affect: she says 'Their genitals will be hundreds of miles away' in a tone of complete bureaucratic reasonableness, as if this is a perfectly normal thing to have to explain. The word 'genitals' in that context is exquisitely chosen — clinical, specific, unashamed. The logic is airtight and that makes it funnier. Comparable to the calibration anchor jokes in construction quality.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie Dart
dialogue.line: Don't be alarmed.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Why would I be alarmed?

dialogue.speaker: Frankie Dart
dialogue.line: Well, it's a robot.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: So? I'm not some luddite who gets scared of robots.

jokes.text: 'From each other?' — Elroy's follow-up confusion
jokes.setup: Frankie says the prisoners' genitals will be hundreds of miles away
jokes.punchline: Elroy mishears/misinterprets this as meaning the genitals will be far from each other (not from the robots), implying he's imagining some horrifying anatomical scattering
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Two words that completely reframe the previous joke and generate a whole new, more disturbing image. Elroy's 'From each other?' implies a grotesque anatomy — the horror of THAT image is what makes the room erupt. Perfect economy (literally two words), and it only works because of the specific setup. This is joke-writing at a very high level.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was... that was really seamless.

jokes.text: 'They're iPads on sticks.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is treating the prisoner robots as a serious threat
jokes.punchline: Jeff reduces the terrifying premise to the mundane physical reality — they're just iPads mounted on sticks
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflation — cutting through pomposity with brutal simplicity. 'iPads on sticks' is a great line, perfectly economical and visually accurate.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: I'm not comfortable with this. We're giving robots to prisoners? That's how you get a robot uprising. I've seen enough movies to know how this ends.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: And before you say anything, yes, I know I'm the skeptical black guy. That's my thing. But I'm right about this one.

jokes.text: 'Hey, guys. I'm moonwalking.' — a prisoner bot moonwalking past mid-argument
jokes.setup: Serious debate about whether to allow prisoner robots in the school
jokes.punchline: A robot casually rolls by moonwalking, completely undercutting the gravity of the conversation
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing — the moonwalking robot mid-serious-argument is a great visual gag. The casualness of 'Hey, guys. I'm moonwalking' as a drive-by is very funny. Demonstrates the comedic potential of the episode's premise immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We have prisoners on campus for the work-study program, and I'm concerned about safety.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You're right to be concerned. What if they sexually assault someone?

jokes.text: 'Jeffrey, you know, ordinarily I'd do anything you say.' / 'Do it. Let's do it.' / 'Well, I walked into that one.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is about to explain why he wouldn't just follow Jeff's advice this time
jokes.punchline: Jeff interrupts with 'Do it. Let's do it.' — exploiting the Dean's established devotion — and the Dean ruefully admits he set himself up
jokes.explanation: Good Dean/Jeff dynamic joke. Jeff weaponizes the Dean's obsequiousness with minimal effort, and 'Well, I walked into that one' is a great self-aware button. Character-specific — this exact joke only works with these two.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: I'm worried about prisoner rape.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, if they're robots, they don't have the biological capacity for sexual assault. Their programming is strictly custodial.

jokes.text: 'Gross! Who farted? Oh, wait, never mind.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of the serious vote about prisoner robots
jokes.punchline: A completely random fart alarm/false alarm — the casual 'Oh, wait, never mind' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's weakest jokes. A random fart reference with no character specificity, no setup, and no payoff beyond the interruption itself. 'Oh, wait, never mind' at least has a mild absurdist beat (the mystery is never explained) but this is filler-level comedy that relies on random = funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: We need to be concerned about dangerous convicts in our community.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? They're not dangerous, they're just like... regular people.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Jeff, these are convicted felons we're discussing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, but if you think about it, they're basically just iPads with abandonment issues.

jokes.text: 'If I'm running the school, pay me more.' / 'What if I made you professor emeritus?' / 'Does it pay more?' / 'No.' / 'Then give me what the ceremony would cost.'
jokes.setup: The Dean offers Jeff a ceremonial honor (professor emeritus) as compensation
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pure economic pragmatism — immediately asking if it pays more, then requesting the cost of the ceremony itself when the answer is no
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest exchanges. The logic of 'give me what the ceremony would cost' is brilliantly Jeff — he reduces everything to mercenary calculus, refuses all sentiment, and his ask is both completely reasonable AND reveals how hollow the honor is. Excellent structure (three-beat: offer → check → redirect) and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm moonwalking on my robot.

jokes.text: 'Now, if I see any race gangs forming, I will have no choice but to adjust the contrasts on your screens until you all look the same.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is welcoming prisoner robots to Greendale and listing his policies
jokes.punchline: His 'anti-racism' policy is to make everyone look the same by adjusting screen contrast — a technically feasible but completely wrongheaded solution that inadvertently parodies colorblindness ideology
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever — the Dean's solution is both hilariously literal (he CAN adjust contrast) and a perfect satire of 'I don't see color' colorblind ideology. It's exactly the kind of joke only Pelton can deliver because his oblivious earnestness makes it land rather than offend. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Do it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I walked right into that, didn't I?

jokes.text: 'And we have a very strict No Bullying policy that relates directly to me, so be nice... to me.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is listing school policies for the new prisoner-robot students
jokes.punchline: He reveals the anti-bullying policy is personal — it's specifically about people being mean to him
jokes.explanation: Good Dean joke — his narcissistic self-pity is perfectly in character. 'Be nice... to me' is a good reveal beat. Not exceptional but solidly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, I can see you, I can hear you, I can even feel the vibrations through my sensors, but... I can't smell anything.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What kind of half-baked telepresence technology doesn't include smell?

jokes.text: 'That's very folksy. Thank you.' — Frankie's dry response to a prisoner's sincere speech
jokes.setup: A prisoner robot gives a sincere, plainspoken speech about rehabilitation ('we ain't here to do any more')
jokes.punchline: Frankie acknowledges it with 'very folksy' — patronizing in the most polite possible way, reducing the genuine moment to a tone note
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frankie line — she can't help being clinical even during moments of genuine connection. 'That's very folksy' is specific and funny, and 'Thank you' makes it even funnier by acknowledging the inappropriateness without correcting it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so this Professor Emeritus thing doesn't come with a raise?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It's an honor, Jeff. A ceremonial recognition of your years of service.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Right, but honor doesn't pay my mortgage. How much is the ceremony budget?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Approximately three thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Perfect. I'll take it in cash.

jokes.text: 'No one at this school should pick on any class of people. It's like watching magicians bully jugglers.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is breaking up bullying of the prisoner robots by regular students
jokes.punchline: His analogy — 'magicians bullying jugglers' — hilariously frames both groups (students and prisoner-bots) as equally low-status circus performers, so the hierarchy is meaningless
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent line. The specificity of 'magicians bully jugglers' is what makes it — both groups ARE slightly pathetic, so the internal hierarchy is absurd. It's also Jeff at his most eloquently lazy: a surprisingly insightful observation delivered as a throwaway. High originality, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to address the racial tension in our prison program before it becomes a real problem.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I've implemented a simple solution: I've adjusted all the monitors in the prison to black and white.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: If they can't see race, they can't be racist.

jokes.text: 'I was a phony lawyer. I got caught, and now I teach a pretty phony class. It's an automatic A. But you might learn a thing or two. And I mean, literally, a thing or two.'
jokes.setup: Willy asks Jeff if he can teach him how to get out of prison
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-deprecating intro to his teaching philosophy is both honest and absurdist — 'literally, a thing or two' is a great kicker specifying that the class's educational content maxes out at two things
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff self-awareness — he's fully aware he's fraudulent and doesn't hide it. 'Literally, a thing or two' as a beat following the conventional phrase is a well-constructed comic deflation. Fits the character perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: At Greendale, we have a very strict anti-bullying policy. We believe that every student deserves to feel safe and respected on campus.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: In fact, this policy is so important to me, I've made it my personal mission to ensure it's enforced... particularly when it comes to protecting myself from mean comments about my cardigan collection.

jokes.text: 'And they call me the criminal.'
jokes.setup: Jeff admits he was a phony lawyer who faked credentials and now teaches an automatic-A class
jokes.punchline: Willy's dry aside points out that Jeff's white-collar fraud is arguably comparable to whatever put Willy in prison
jokes.explanation: Very economical — the line is a classic irony beat. Not highly original (the 'and they call ME the bad guy' construction is old) but perfectly placed and delivered with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so we're picking on prisoners? That's like one marginally skilled group bullying another.

jokes.text: 'Trust me. I know the main difference between us is an orange jumpsuit. And you have an iPad!'
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a sincere statement about their moral equivalence (the jumpsuit line)
jokes.punchline: Willy's addendum 'And you have an iPad!' punctures Jeff's philosophizing with a mundane material observation — the conversation is happening via robot screen
jokes.explanation: Good joke structure — Jeff's sincere moment gets undercut by a material truth (the robot medium), which also advances the episode's theme about presence vs. technology. The joke works on two levels.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I appreciate the sentiment, but I have to be honest with you - my law degree is from an online university that no longer exists, I've never actually passed the bar, and I'm pretty sure half the stuff I've told people about my legal experience was made up on the spot.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, and I'm a murderer.' — Willy's casual self-identification
jokes.setup: Light banter about Jeff having an iPad advantage
jokes.punchline: Willy pivots completely to 'and I'm a murderer' — delivered so casually it becomes absurd
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan — the casualness of 'I'm a murderer' as a conversation point is funny. Sets up the episode's dark-comedy throughline about murder being something you just carry with you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You might learn one or two things in my class.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And I mean exactly two things. Not the idiom. Literally two things. That's all you're getting.

jokes.text: 'You know, once you take another man's life, the least you could do is carry it with you.'
jokes.setup: Willy acknowledges being a murderer without pride
jokes.punchline: His moral philosophy about murder — 'carry it with you' — is delivered as folk wisdom, profound-sounding but also just describing basic moral responsibility in the most banal way
jokes.explanation: Genuinely good line — it sounds like wisdom but it's also the minimum acceptable response to murder. The gap between the gravity of murder and the folksy delivery creates a funny, unsettling tone. Good character work for Willy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm a fraud. I never actually went to high school.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: At least you went to college.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't go to college either. I forged my transcripts to get into this school.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you're a criminal, and I'm the one they kicked out?

jokes.text: 'Are you carrying any murders, Mr. Winger?' — Willy asking Jeff as a sincere question
jokes.setup: Willy has established murder as something you 'carry with you' philosophically
jokes.punchline: He turns it into a sincere inquiry directed at Jeff — as if asking about murders is as normal as asking about baggage
jokes.explanation: Good dark-comedy line. The normalization of murder as a conversational subject is the joke — asking about it like it's a hobby. The beat pause before Jeff's 'I am not' response makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, Willy, when you really think about it, we're not that different. We both want respect, we both want to be seen as more than just our circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: That's beautiful, man.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Right? I mean, strip away the designer clothes, the law degree, the chiseled jawline—

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: And you're basically me.

jokes.text: 'I hear you have to have strong feelings for someone you kill. I try to reserve that stuff for myself.'
jokes.setup: Willy's murder philosophy prompts Jeff to reflect on his own emotional patterns
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'I reserve strong feelings for myself' is a simultaneously dark self-diagnosis (narcissism preventing him from deep connections) played as casual deflection
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. Jeff's narcissism is a central character trait, and this line encapsulates it in a weirdly eloquent dark-comedy way. 'I try to reserve that stuff for myself' as a reason he wouldn't murder anyone is both funny and genuinely revealing. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're basically the same, except for the jumpsuit.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: And the fact that I'm a figment of your imagination.

jokes.text: 'Oh, look! Ice worlds. Oh, the majesty. Rhinos and elephants and fiamingos.'
jokes.setup: Jeff puts on Planet Earth for his class of prisoners
jokes.punchline: 'Fiamingos' (flamingos mispronounced) — delivered with genuine wonder — suggests these are men who don't often see nature documentaries, and their childlike awe is both funny and touching
jokes.explanation: 'Fiamingos' is a good touch — the mispronunciation grounds the absurdist premise with character detail. The prisoners' genuine delight at Planet Earth is funny and endearing simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I killed a man.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But I'm not proud of it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: See, the thing is, if you're going to kill a man, you gotta own it. You can't go around feeling guilty about your murders. That's not taking responsibility, that's just being a coward.

jokes.text: Abed's meta-commentary on 'pop back gags': 'I'd like to make this moment worth popping back to from some point in the future. I don't know what that means. There. Don't worry. It'll pay off.'
jokes.setup: Abed is discussing who has seniority in the apartment; Britta claims she was first
jokes.punchline: Abed reveals he used to deliberately plant moments for future callbacks — then explains the mechanics to Annie, acknowledges she doesn't understand, and assures her it'll pay off anyway
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best meta moments. Abed is explicitly describing his own role as a storytelling device within the show — he used to plant callbacks deliberately for future narrative use. 'I don't know what that means. There. Don't worry. It'll pay off.' is a brilliant three-beat that explains, enacts, and predicts the gag simultaneously. This could only be Abed. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: I have a philosophy about carrying murders. You only carry the murders you can handle.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: Jeff, how many murders are you carrying?

jokes.text: 'They're like conventions for every subject too boring to have their own convention. And instead of Joss Whedon, the police show up.'
jokes.setup: Abed explains why he doesn't get anything out of parties
jokes.punchline: His analogy compares parties to bad conventions — with the kicker that the 'celebrity guest' at a party is the police
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and one of the best Abed lines in the season. The analogy is completely original, perfectly structured, and could only come from someone who thinks in pop-culture frameworks. 'Instead of Joss Whedon, the police show up' is brilliant — it's funny on its own AND the inversion (cool celebrity → cops) perfectly captures why parties are disappointing for someone like Abed. Highly quotable, highly rewatch-valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I can't even commit murder. It requires too much emotional investment. I'd have to care about someone enough to want them dead, and frankly, most people aren't worth the effort.

jokes.text: 'The police also showed up when you made Leonard take off his clothes and filled the living room with lizards. That was for my movie, Reverse Godzilla.'
jokes.setup: Britta points out that Abed's presence also attracts the police
jokes.punchline: Abed's matter-of-fact explanation: he made Leonard strip and filled the apartment with lizards for a movie called 'Reverse Godzilla' — both the detail and the title are insane
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. 'Reverse Godzilla' as a title is funny on its own (what does it mean?), but the specific image of Leonard stripping among lizards is both absurd and absolutely in-character for Abed's filmmaking. The 'I also thought it might make a good pop back' kicker adds a meta-layer, calling back joke #41.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So... that murder thing. Pretty crazy, right? I mean, obviously murder is bad. Very bad. The worst, really.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Anyway! Did you know that the African elephant is the largest land mammal? Fascinating creatures. They can communicate over distances of up to six miles using infrasound. Nature is truly amazing!

jokes.text: 'Annie makes rules. You make parties. Her rules cancel out your parties, but I'm not involved. I just make movies.'
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to get Abed to overrule Annie's party rules
jokes.punchline: Abed delivers a formal, syllogistic dismissal of the conflict — framing himself as above it all by virtue of making movies — with a final 'I just make movies' that is both absurd self-importance and accurate
jokes.explanation: Great Abed logic — he treats the apartment dynamics like a game theory problem and opts out by declaring a separate jurisdiction. 'I just make movies' as the final word is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I used to do this thing where I'd set up a joke in the pilot, then call it back later in the season. It was very meta.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But then I realized I was spending so much time setting up callbacks that I wasn't actually making jokes in the present moment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So now I just make jokes. And if they happen to callback to something, great. If not, that's also great, because at least I'm not trapped in a narrative structure of my own design.

jokes.text: 'Slick words. Cock of the walk. What are categories in Prison Jeopardy?'
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a smooth, sarcastic comment about his car
jokes.punchline: Willy reframes Jeff's verbal style as Prison Jeopardy categories — positioning Jeff's rhetorical coolness as a jailhouse game-show genre
jokes.explanation: 'Prison Jeopardy' is a great comic concept — Willy is both mocking Jeff's verbal posturing AND creating a whole imaginary game show in one line. Good economy and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pop back gags are a sitcom staple where a character reappears after being written out, usually with an explanation that subverts expectations. The meta-humor comes from acknowledging the trope itself.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But I've been doing this so much that I've stopped actually being meta and just... became the thing I was making fun of. Now I'm just mechanically aware of tropes instead of genuinely commenting on them.

jokes.text: Willy lures Jeff to look down the stairs under the pretense of a lost ball bearing — the slapstick near-murder attempt
jokes.setup: Willy asks Jeff to help find a 'lost ball bearing' that rolled down some stairs
jokes.punchline: The ball bearing is an obvious ruse — Willy's trying to push Jeff down stairs — which Jeff realizes just in time
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom dark comedy — a robot trying to murder someone by luring them to stairs is inherently absurd, and the mundanity of 'lost a ball bearing' as the cover story is funny. The comedy escalates through Jeff's dawning realization.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Parties are just conventions for boring subjects. Like how action movies have explosions, parties have small talk. They're both just filler to distract you from the lack of real content.

jokes.text: 'Did you just try to murder me?' / [pause] 'Are you trying to murder me?' / [pause] 'You're trying as hard as you can right now to kill me.'
jokes.setup: Jeff narrowly avoids being pushed down stairs by Willy's robot
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dawning realization plays out in three escalating sentences — each one a slightly more committed statement of the obvious, punctuated by pauses as the absurdity compounds
jokes.explanation: Good escalation structure — three questions/statements of increasing certainty, each separated by a beat. 'You're trying as hard as you can right now to kill me' is a great final version, implying Jeff is evaluating Willy's murder effort level. The specificity of 'as hard as you can' is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We could fill the entire apartment with lizards. It would be like a low-budget Jurassic Park, except the dinosaurs are just regular lizards and instead of running from them, we're living with them.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not a bad pitch. 'Lizard House.' Coming this summer to a streaming service that desperately needs content.

jokes.text: 'Okay, well, uh, I guess I'll see you in class tomorrow? Guy who tried to murder me?'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just realized Willy tried to murder him
jokes.punchline: He says goodbye anyway — with an awkward normalcy — as if social convention demands he still be polite to a person who just tried to kill him
jokes.explanation: Very good joke — the comedy is in Jeff defaulting to social normalcy even after a murder attempt. 'Guy who tried to murder me?' as an appended clarification is a perfect beat. Very Community — the mundane and the violent are treated with equal casual affect.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Everyone in this apartment can be reduced to simple mathematical functions. Troy is a linear function—predictable, consistent. Shirley's a polynomial—complex, with multiple peaks and valleys. Annie's exponential—she grows exponentially with stress. Jeff is a constant—he never changes, he just stays cool. Britta's a logarithm—diminishing returns on every decision she makes. And I'm the function that describes all the other functions.

jokes.text: Britta has thrown a party under cover of a 'film' called 'Britta's Party, Based on a True Story of Fun and No Rules' — the reveal of the script
jokes.setup: Annie comes home to find a party being set up
jokes.punchline: Abed holds up a 'script' called 'Britta's Party, Based on a True Story' — the film's existence as a legal fiction to get around Annie's rules
jokes.explanation: Very good concept joke — using 'it's a film' as a legal loophole to have a party is completely in-character for Abed and Britta. The formal script with title card is a great visual element.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Willy, you can't just use prison slang like that in everyday conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: What do you mean? 'Shank,' 'Lockdown,' 'Yard Time' — these are perfectly good words.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Those are prison terms, Willy. You sound like you're hosting a game show.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: For $200: A stabbing implement made from a toothbrush. What is a shank?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: See? That's exactly what I'm talking about.

jokes.text: 'I see the real-time stakes of Can't Hardly Wait, the subversive raunch of Risky Business, and the mumbly pointlessness of everything after 2003.'
jokes.setup: Abed pitches his party film vision to Annie
jokes.punchline: The critical breakdown of the film's lineage is very Abed, but 'the mumbly pointlessness of everything after 2003' is a pointed dismissal of mumblecore/indie film that doubles as self-deprecating humor about Abed-style movies
jokes.explanation: Very good Abed line. The progression (Can't Hardly Wait → Risky Business → 'mumbly pointlessness of everything after 2003') is well-structured, and the final item is a funny self-aware dig at the kind of films Abed tends to make. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Did you just try to push me down the stairs?

jokes.text: 'Don't look at me. I could never greenlight a project this big. I moved in third. I'm a coucher.' / Group: 'She's a coucher! I sleep... on a couch! Oh, she's a coucher!'
jokes.setup: Britta tries to deflect responsibility for the party-film scheme
jokes.punchline: The 'coucher' chant returns with even more energy and variations — 'She's a coucher!' becoming a group chorus
jokes.explanation: The running gag payoff works well — the group has fully adopted 'coucher' as a chant, and 'Look out! Look out! Who was it? It's the coucher!' adds gleeful mob energy. Running gags earn their score through the momentum they build.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't attempt to murder anyone!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's what someone who attempted murder would say.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, well I'm escalating this to a maximum effort murder attempt.

jokes.text: 'Before this is over, you'll beg for my forgiveness.' — Britta's overdramatic declaration as the party begins
jokes.setup: Britta is being mocked and called a coucher
jokes.punchline: She responds with a melodramatic villain line that is completely disproportionate to the situation — a party argument
jokes.explanation: In-character for Britta's delusional sense of her own heroism. The villain pose is funny given the stakes (a party argument). Functional but not outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oy vey!

jokes.text: 'We have an ultimately low stakes but nonetheless creepy problem with one of our wi-felons.'
jokes.setup: Jeff needs to report Willy's murder attempt to Frankie
jokes.punchline: 'Wi-felons' — a portmanteau of Wi-Fi and felons for the wireless prisoner robots — is a very good coinage
jokes.explanation: 'Wi-felons' is an excellent portmanteau — it's immediately understood, clever, and has a double meaning (Wi-Fi connection + felon). One of the episode's best wordplay moments. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm making a documentary about a party. We're treating it like it's a serious historical event. There's a steadicam following everyone, we have interviews with guests about their motivations, we're analyzing the snack choices as cultural indicators.

jokes.text: 'Did he steal the driver's ed simulator? Did he start an illegal game of solitaire on his face?'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks what else Willy has done on campus
jokes.punchline: His examples are hilariously specific absurdist crimes — especially 'illegal game of solitaire on his face' (using the robot screen as a card game surface?)
jokes.explanation: 'Illegal game of solitaire on his face' is a great absurdist detail — it's specific enough to be funny even though it barely makes sense. Good Jeff energy — he's constructing crimes that are both petty and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Boy meets girl. Boy loses girl. Boy gets girl back. Girl leaves boy for a astronaut.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No wait, scratch that last part. Boy meets girl. Boy loses girl. Boy gets girl back. The end.

jokes.text: 'Jeffrey, he's in the room.' / 'Hey, Mr. Winger.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is telling Frankie that Willy tried to murder him — not knowing Willy's robot is on Frankie's laptop
jokes.punchline: Willy has been listening the whole time and greets Jeff cheerfully
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom embarrassment setup — talking about someone who can hear you. 'Hey, Mr. Winger' is a perfect, economical punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My film draws from Godard, Truffaut, and early Soderbergh. It's a meditation on alienation in the digital age, shot entirely in natural light with a handheld camera aesthetic.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But honestly, these modern mumblecore films are just bad acting hidden behind a veil of authenticity. They call it 'naturalistic' when really the actors just forgot their lines.

jokes.text: Hey, Mr. Winger. [Willy is watching from the laptop]
jokes.setup: Frankie has just told Jeff that Willy is in the room
jokes.punchline: Willy's breezy 'Hey, Mr. Winger' — delivered as if this is completely normal — is the comedic payoff; his casual civility after a murder attempt is the joke
jokes.explanation: Willy's affable 'Hey, Mr. Winger' after a murder attempt is funny because it's the same civilized classroom register he's maintained throughout — the contrast between his actions and his manner is the character's core comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Fine, I guess I don't get a say in this apartment anyway. I'm just the permissive pothead with no backbone.

jokes.text: 'Well, have you ever killed anyone, Jeffrey? Why would an actual murderer want to kill a community college teacher? Now I'm not worth murdering?'
jokes.setup: Frankie dismisses Jeff's murder accusation; Jeff responds
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Now I'm not worth murdering?' — his ego is wounded by the suggestion that he's not important enough to be a murder target
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The progression is perfect: Frankie's logic is 'why would a murderer target you?' and Jeff's vanity converts this into an insult about his importance. 'Now I'm not worth murdering?' is a great line — it's about Jeff's ego, not safety. Very high character integration, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Fine! I'm a coucher. I couch.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You couch so hard.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I couch so hard.

jokes.text: 'Isn't that your specialty? You're a raconteur. You charm people with your slick and fancy words. Willy... Willy just charms them.'
jokes.setup: Jeff accuses Willy of charming Frankie; Willy turns it back on Jeff
jokes.punchline: Willy's self-description — 'I just charm them' (versus Jeff's verbal tricks) — implies Willy charms through simplicity/authenticity while Jeff needs words, which also inadvertently admits Willy is manipulating Frankie
jokes.explanation: Good character dynamics — the Jeff vs. Willy verbal sparring works because both are manipulators with different styles. 'Willy just charms them' is a funny contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. I'm done being the nice one. I'm done compromising. You want to see what happens when Annie Edison stops being nice? Because I can make things very difficult for all of you. Very difficult.

jokes.text: 'Jealousy isn't a crime, Jeffrey, but costing the school $300,000 will be.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is jealous that Willy is charming Frankie; Frankie dismisses his concerns
jokes.punchline: Frankie reduces Jeff's grievance to 'jealousy' and immediately pivots to financial consequences — characteristically prioritizing budget over emotional concerns
jokes.explanation: Good Frankie line — she always cuts through to financial/institutional reality. 'Jealousy isn't a crime, but costing the school $300,000 will be' is well-constructed with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: What else did Willy do?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He used an iPad to hack into the Pentagon.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Okay, that's bad.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Then he used an iPad to commit identity theft.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: That's worse.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Then he used an iPad to teach dolphins how to use iPads.

jokes.text: 'Which is why they call it "yard juice"' — mid-sentence snippet from a prison story being told to Jeff's class
jokes.setup: Jeff's class is bonding with the prisoner-bots; Jeff walks in on a story already in progress
jokes.punchline: The punchline to some unknown prison story is 'yard juice' — left completely unexplained, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: In medias punchline is a great comedy technique — dropping into a conversation at the exact moment of its most absurd conclusion. 'Yard juice' is funny precisely because we don't know what it means and the story is never explained.

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: Well now, I didn't mean nothin' by it. Back where I come from, we just say things the way they are. If a fella's got a little extra melanin, that's just the good Lord's way of—

jokes.text: 'Does anyone ever get their head stuck between the bars? We call it getting metal ears.'
jokes.setup: Students are asking prisoner-bots innocent questions about prison life
jokes.punchline: 'Getting metal ears' as a prison term for getting your head stuck in bars — a weirdly specific and vivid piece of invented prison slang
jokes.explanation: Good invented prison slang — 'metal ears' is specific enough to feel authentic (the visual of ears sticking through bars) while being funny. The question itself ('does anyone ever get their head stuck in the bars?') is funny for its earnest naivety.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, why would a murderer kill a teacher? What, I'm not murder-worthy enough?

jokes.text: Jeff's pseudo-folksy law lecture: 'I don't cotton much to fancy words and book study. It's not how I got to where I am.' / 'How did you get to where you are, Mr. Winger?' / 'Mr. Winger was born in dirt, Willy. Same as you, I'm sure. And I had my face held down in that dirt by the kings of dirt.'
jokes.setup: Jeff decides to lecture without notes, going full self-mythologizing mode — adopting Willy's folksy speech patterns back at him
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'kings of dirt' speech is simultaneously Jeff at his most self-aggrandizing AND a parody of his own rhetoric — his attempt to out-Willy Willy by being even more rural-sage
jokes.explanation: Jeff doing a parody of Jeff — adopting Willy's rhetorical style and amplifying it into absurdity ('kings of dirt') is a great character moment. 'I got out. By talking. By lying.' is also good self-aware character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff is such a raconteur.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, it's pronounced 'rock n tour.'

jokes.text: Mr. Winger was born in dirt, Willy. Same as you, I'm sure. And I had my face held down in that dirt by the kings of dirt. And now, they're still there, ruling over dirt, and I... got out. By talking. By lying.
jokes.setup: Willy has asked how Jeff got to where he is; Jeff starts to give a heroic answer
jokes.punchline: The 'kings of dirt' escalation followed by 'got out. By talking. By lying.' — the heroic monologue collapses into self-deflation. Jeff builds himself up in mythic terms only to admit his method was deception
jokes.explanation: 'Kings of dirt' is an absurdly grandiose metaphor for high school bullies, and the speech is structured to build heroically before collapsing into 'by talking. By lying.' The collapse is the joke. Jeff's self-mythologizing combined with his self-awareness is the character at its comedic best. The speech structure (build/deflation) is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I mean, who needs to know the technical legal definition of anything? I'm a lawyer and I teach at a community college, so clearly education isn't that important.

jokes.text: 'Mr. Winger, when did you stop being funny? I mean, am I wrong, or does he seem really intense here? Like, "Ah, you were born in the dirt and you'll die in the dirt. Kings... and then, who are the kings of the dirt?"'
jokes.setup: Jeff's melodramatic dirt speech has killed the room
jokes.punchline: Garrett, a minor background character, calls out that Jeff has gotten too serious — the meta-commentary from the most unexpected source is very funny
jokes.explanation: Garrett calling out Jeff's tonal shift is a great meta moment — the show acknowledging that Jeff has gone too serious via the most insignificant character. His impression of Jeff ('you were born in the dirt and you'll die in the dirt') is a funny recap. High character integration for Garrett.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm just a simple man from humble dirt origins. My father was dirt, my mother was dirt. I was born in a dirt hospital, delivered by a dirt doctor.

jokes.text: 'Shouldn't have worn that petard if you didn't want to be hoisted by it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is complaining that everyone is charmed by Willy because he championed the program
jokes.punchline: Elroy misapplies the 'hoist by your own petard' idiom — reframing 'petard' as a fashion item to wear, rather than an explosive device
jokes.explanation: Good wordplay — treating 'petard' as clothing is a simple but effective misinterpretation. Sets up the following much better joke.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Did anyone else notice Jeff suddenly became competent at something?

jokes.text: Jeff asks what 'hoisted by your own petard' means, and Elroy speculates: 'I guess I just assumed that in the old days, a petard was a special outfit, like a leotard, with a lot of fancy buckles and loops on it and that rich people would wear them when they were feeling especially smug, but then poor people could tie a rope to one of the loops and hoist them up a pole and then let them dangle there as punishment for being cocky.'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks what Elroy thinks 'hoisted by your own petard' means
jokes.punchline: Elroy's entirely invented, completely plausible-sounding etymology — a leotard-like garment for smugness, with built-in hoisting loops — is delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best in the series. Elroy's explanation is both absurdly detailed and oddly coherent — it has internal logic (loops for hoisting, a specific social class wearing it, punishment for cockiness). The image of a leotard designed for public humiliation is vivid and hilarious. 'Never look it up. Your explanation is way better' is the perfect button — the joke rewards Elroy's invention over reality. This is craft-forward comedy at its finest.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I can't believe this. I fought so hard to get this program approved, and now it's completely backfiring on me.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Well, you know what they say — you're being hoist by your own petard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? I'm being hoisted by my own... petard? What is a petard?

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: It's an explosive device from medieval times. The phrase means you're suffering from your own plan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're saying I'm literally being blown up by a medieval bomb that I created?

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: No, it's just a metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I'm pretty sure I would remember building a bomb.

jokes.text: 'Never look it up. Your explanation is way better.'
jokes.setup: Elroy has given an elaborate fake etymology for 'petard'
jokes.punchline: Jeff endorses the fantasy over fact — a perfect button that affirms the absurdist logic
jokes.explanation: Perfect button — in six words Jeff both completes the joke and makes a broader anti-intellectual statement. Works as a standalone line AND as a payoff for Elroy's speech.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Wait, what do you mean 'hoist by your own petard'? That's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: A petard is obviously a medieval French nobleman who specialized in self-sabotage. So if you were 'hoisted by your own petard,' it meant that Petard showed up at your castle and made you look foolish through his elaborate pranks.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: The phrase fell out of use after Petard retired to the countryside and took up cheese-making instead.

jokes.text: 'Jeff, we're having a Britta party here. Could you be a little bit less of a buzzkill?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is brooding at the party about the Willy situation
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'a Britta party' is funny — given that Britta is the least fun member of the group, her party being the benchmark for fun Jeff is ruining is ironic
jokes.explanation: The irony of Britta — Community's designated buzzkill — calling Jeff a buzzkill at 'a Britta party' is good character comedy. Functional and in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that's not what a petard is? Because I've been picturing this whole thing completely differently, and honestly, your version is way less fun.

jokes.text: 'That was great. Now party like there's no tomorrow.' / 'What? There's no tomorrow. Party like it.'
jokes.setup: Partygoers are going about normal party activities
jokes.punchline: Abed directs the party like a film set — 'party like there's no tomorrow, there IS no tomorrow, party like it' — his literal interpretation of the phrase as a directorial instruction is very funny
jokes.explanation: Good Abed joke — he's trying to direct the party's emotional experience using the film premise. 'There's no tomorrow. Party like it.' is an existentially funny instruction delivered with complete directorial authority.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, no, no! You're not getting it. This is a party scene. People at parties don't just stand there reciting lines like robots.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You need to interact, to be present, to actually BE at a party. It's method acting, people!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why is this so hard? I'm literally just asking you to do what you do every weekend.

jokes.text: 'Did someone order a prison break? Plenty of convicts to go around.'
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives at the party with prisoner robots as surprise guests
jokes.punchline: His framing of prisoner robots as party favors — 'plenty of convicts to go around,' 'pass 'em around!' — treats them as entertainment commodities
jokes.explanation: Good Dean moment — his oblivious enthusiasm for the worst ideas is endearing and funny. 'Did someone order a prison break?' is a solid line.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm not going to bust you for having a party. I'm way too cool for that.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But I am going to ask you to keep it down because I have a very important breakfast meeting tomorrow morning, and I need my beauty sleep. Which, let's be honest, I need a lot of.

jokes.text: 'Take them to the dance floor! Pass 'em around! That's Willy, pass him! Over here. Pass Willy. Pass me Willy.'
jokes.setup: Prisoner robots at a party
jokes.punchline: The robots are literally being crowd-surfed/passed around the party — the visual of iPads on sticks being handed through a crowd like party objects
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag — the image of prisoner robots being crowd-surfed is inherently hilarious and extends the episode's premise in an unexpected direction. Impact score reflects the visual comedy that the transcript can only partially convey.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'd like you to meet our new party entertainment—prisoner robots!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: They're programmed to simulate maximum security prison conditions, but don't worry—it's all in good fun!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Who wants to experience solitary confinement? It's like a spa day, but with more psychological trauma!

jokes.text: 'Oh, crap. This is it. Keep doing that.'
jokes.setup: Willy's robot is being passed around at the party while he observes from prison
jokes.punchline: Willy's reaction — 'Oh crap. This is it. Keep doing that.' — implies this prison-man is experiencing genuine transcendence at being crowd-surfed via robot, which is both funny and oddly touching
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny and unexpectedly affecting — Willy's 'This is it' suggests real joy at a moment of connection mediated through technology. 'Keep doing that' is a perfect, economical response. The dark comedy of a murderer's transcendent moment being robot crowd-surfing works very well.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, I need you to treat dancing as measurable effort. I want to see sweat. I want to see commitment. This isn't just moving your body to music—this is a cinematic experience.

jokes.text: 'Try dancing harder. Is that as hard as you can dance? You're at a party. You're celebrating!'
jokes.setup: Abed is directing his documentary-party film
jokes.punchline: He's coaching party guests on how to dance more authentically — the impossibility of directing genuine fun
jokes.explanation: Good Abed joke — the meta-absurdity of directing people to 'be more fun' captures the central theme of the Britta party subplot. 'Is that as hard as you can dance?' is a funny directorial note.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why are you all dancing like it's 1987? This party is supposed to be happening now.

jokes.text: 'Abed, it's 6:00 in the morning.' / 'Okay, thanks.'
jokes.setup: Abed is still trying to get authentic party footage at dawn
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, thanks' — Abed receives the information about the time and immediately moves on without changing behavior, as if it's data received but irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Very economical Abed joke — 'Okay, thanks' as a full response to 'it's 6am and you're still filming' is perfect. He acknowledges the information and continues. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You think I'm not a real killer? I've killed plenty of people. I killed a guy in a parking lot once. Well, I didn't kill him, but I definitely contributed to his death.

jokes.text: 'Nobody's partied like there's no tomorrow yet. They keep dancing like it's today.'
jokes.setup: Abed is frustrated that his film isn't capturing the transcendent party moment
jokes.punchline: 'They keep dancing like it's today' — a great inversion. The absence of tomorrow as a concept is surprisingly philosophically rich as a comedy line
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Abed lines. 'They keep dancing like it's today' is the kind of absurdist observation that works on multiple levels — it's literally what people do (dance in the present), it's a funny film-director complaint, and it accidentally articulates something true about how people relate to mortality. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Willy, Willy, can you hear me? Willy?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I think you're losing him.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Willy, stay with me. Don't go into the light!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, I think the WiFi just went out.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that explains the afterlife.

jokes.text: 'I think it's a performance issue. I think this needed some real actors.' / 'Well, lesson learned.'
jokes.setup: The party-film isn't working because real people aren't performing authentically
jokes.punchline: Abed concludes he needed 'real actors' for a documentary about a real party — which inverts the entire concept of documentary filmmaking
jokes.explanation: Good meta-joke about documentary vs. performance. Abed's conclusion that authentic people make bad documentary subjects is a funny philosophical inversion. 'Well, lesson learned' from Britta is a perfect, resigned button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why don't you look up dignity?

dialogue.speaker: Willy
dialogue.line: I can't. My tablet's destroyed and I'm emotionally damaged.

jokes.text: Abed brings in professional actors to 'party naturally' at the film's climax
jokes.setup: The party film needs authentic footage of partying
jokes.punchline: Abed hires professionals to simulate authenticity — the logical extreme of his controlling directorial vision
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist escalation — the natural conclusion of Abed's obsession taken to its extreme. Works as character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're living in an RV? Where do you... you know... go to the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: There's a toilet in the back.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But where does it go?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Into a tank underneath. You have to empty it manually.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I have questions.

jokes.text: 'Well, Willy, look at me. I'm a murderer. Can I be as cool as you now?'
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts Willy at the party about the murder attempt
jokes.punchline: Jeff's sarcastic claim to murderer-cool — recognizing that Willy has used his status to outmaneuver Jeff — is a good character moment
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jeff recognizes the social dynamics have inverted, with a murderer having more cache than him. In-character and funny, though not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Living in an RV? That's basically being homeless.

dialogue.speaker: Homeless Person
dialogue.line: Yeah, well at least I don't have to worry about my septic tank backing up into my shower.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He's got a point.

jokes.text: Willy's screen goes dark/dies — 'Willy, focus on my voice. Hey, I'm losing you.' / 'You're not losing me!' / 'You are going to a better place with a stronger signal!'
jokes.setup: Willy's robot is being destroyed/damaged in the party chaos
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'dying' speech — 'you are going to a better place with a stronger signal' — applies death-drama language to a robot going offline, with 'stronger signal' as a parody of 'better place'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'You are going to a better place with a stronger signal' is the perfect technological reframe of a death platitude. The 'better place' cliché gets a Wi-Fi twist that works on two levels: it's funny as a death parody AND it comments on the whole episode's theme of connection vs. technology. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right, Annie. I'm sorry. From now on, I'm going to follow every single rule you make. No questions asked. I'll be the most obedient person in this study group.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yes. In fact, I'm getting you a little bell so you can summon me whenever you need something. And I'll curtsy.

jokes.text: Jeff insists 'I'll go on my own, with dignity. Something you should look up!' / 'I can't look it up! You destroyed my device!'
jokes.setup: Jeff claims dignity in his dismissal from campus
jokes.punchline: He tells the Dean to 'look up' dignity — but the Dean's literal ability to look things up has been destroyed (the robot/device Jeff smashed)
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed — Jeff's rhetorical 'look it up' is turned literal because he just destroyed the device the Dean would have used to do so. The callback is tight and the structure is excellent. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need to get on campus.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're going to need a robot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Why would I need a robot?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, first you need wheels, then a motor, then a gyroscope for balance, then a solar panel for power, then a small nuclear reactor as a backup, then a quantum processor, then—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, stop. I'm just going to walk.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your funeral.

jokes.text: 'Sorry I'm late. I couldn't find a parking spot for my house.' / 'Oh, it must be so cool living in a vehicle, man... Wait, where does your poop go?' / 'A tank.' / 'Gross. Get a house.' / 'Ben, aren't you homeless?' / 'Yeah, but I poop in a house.' / 'Whose?' / 'Nice try.'
jokes.setup: Chang arrives late because he lives in an RV
jokes.punchline: The poop logistics discussion escalates into the reveal that Chang poops in someone else's house — and refuses to say whose
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation — 'where does your poop go?' → 'a tank' → 'gross, get a house' → 'you're also homeless, Ben' → 'yeah but I poop in a house' → 'whose?' → 'nice try.' Each beat builds well and 'Nice try' is a perfect button. The reveal that Chang is secretly using someone's bathroom is a great dark detail.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Parties are just an excuse for people to stand around and pretend they're having fun while actually just checking their phones and wondering when they can leave without seeming rude.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's a collective agreement to waste time together. We're all just hostages in a social contract we never agreed to.

jokes.text: 'Have you learned anything?' / 'Don't question rules. Rules are good. I'm bad. All hail Annie.' / 'Thank you.' / 'Damn.'
jokes.setup: Annie asks Britta if she's learned her lesson about the party
jokes.punchline: Britta gives an exaggeratedly sycophantic capitulation — 'All hail Annie' — and then Annie says 'Thank you' as if this is completely satisfying; then Britta's 'Damn' shows she actually meant it sarcastically
jokes.explanation: Good character exchange — Annie accepting 'All hail Annie' as a sincere apology is funny for her obliviousness, and Britta's 'Damn' shows she actually got what she wanted: Annie's narcissism exposed. Three-beat structure works well.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What will happen to me?

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Something worse than death. Something so terrible, so incomprehensible, that your mind will reject it as impossible.

jokes.text: Oh, nice of you to show up. / We moved here for you. / I didn't ask for this.
jokes.setup: Jeff has arrived at an apartment meeting after being banned from campus
jokes.punchline: 'We moved here for you' is a loaded accusation; 'I didn't ask for this' is the standard selfish-person response that's funny because it's simultaneously true and callous
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Jeff's 'I didn't ask for this' is good in that it captures his selfish streak, but it's not a particularly original joke structure.

dialogue.speaker: Warden
dialogue.line: I now pronounce you husband and wife. And by the power vested in me by the state, I also pronounce you legally bound to perform labor without compensation, as permitted by the 13th Amendment.

jokes.text: 'The dean's making that convict you murdered into a professor.' / 'What? Why do you care?' / 'Because the dean is just doing this to prove something, and it's really stupid.' / 'The guy's dangerous, and he's manipulating him.' / 'Isn't that what you usually do?'
jokes.setup: Jeff objects to Willy being made a professor
jokes.punchline: Annie points out that Jeff's objection to someone manipulating the Dean is rich coming from Jeff, who manipulates the Dean constantly
jokes.explanation: Good character hypocrisy beat — Jeff's jealousy of Willy's manipulation of the Dean is undercut by Annie calling out that Jeff does exactly the same thing. Sets up the subsequent more important exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I've stolen things. Small things. A pen from a hotel, some towels.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But then it got worse. I took a road sign. Then copper wiring from a construction site.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Last week I stole an entire air conditioning unit from the library loading dock.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't even need an air conditioning unit. I just... I couldn't stop myself.

jokes.text: 'No! I mean, yes, but not like that. I lie to the dean for personal gain. I wouldn't use him emotionally. I wouldn't mislead him. I wouldn't hurt him.'
jokes.setup: Annie confronts Jeff about also manipulating the Dean
jokes.punchline: Jeff's distinction between acceptable and unacceptable Dean manipulation is both self-aware and genuinely revealing — he has a code, however twisted
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character moments. Jeff's defense of his Dean manipulation — 'I lie for personal gain, not emotionally' — is hilariously specific and genuinely in-character. It accidentally reveals that Jeff actually cares about the Dean, which is both funny and touching. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not like Willy. I manipulate people, sure, but I do it for me. I'm honest about my selfishness. That's the difference.

jokes.text: 'And yet murderers can.' / 'What have I done? Murderers can get on campus.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is banned from campus but needs to reach the Dean; Willy's murder attempt has recontextualized everything
jokes.punchline: The cosmic injustice — Jeff is banned while actual murderers roam free — stated twice with increasing existential horror
jokes.explanation: 'What have I done? Murderers can get on campus' has a good horror-movie structure — the realization dawning. Good irony beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so Willy's not actually a murderer? I've been feeling superior to him this whole time!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That is so annoying!

jokes.text: 'I'll need a broom, a remote control car, an iPad and an elaborate, gyroscopically stabilized servomotor.' / 'Dude, we're trying to help Jeff here.' / 'You're acting kind of spoiled right now.'
jokes.setup: The group is trying to figure out how to get Jeff back on campus
jokes.punchline: Abed's immediate pivot to building his own telepresence robot — not to help Jeff but as a personal filmmaking project — and Britta calling him spoiled
jokes.explanation: Good Abed character joke — he's already moved past the Jeff problem to his next project. 'Gyroscopically stabilized servomotor' is a funny specific detail. 'You're acting kind of spoiled right now' is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: I don't see why we need to have a meeting about this. We're not robots.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, I've been thinking about robot meetings a lot lately.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Well, I've been thinking about RV harassment, and nobody wants to talk about that.

jokes.text: 'My script is misleading. It's impossible to party like there's no tomorrow. It's based on my desire to have a party. Parties are just booze, low lights, and loud music, so people can feel more, see less, and not have to listen to each other or themselves.'
jokes.setup: Abed wants Britta to give a speech to reinspire the party
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'speech' is a comprehensive debunking of parties and of her own desire for one — she accidentally articulates why parties are inherently sad
jokes.explanation: Good Britta character moment — she's simultaneously right about parties and completely missing the point of enjoying them. The triple construction ('feel more, see less, not listen to each other or themselves') is nicely crafted. Accidentally the most honest thing she says all episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My robot is broken!

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: What happened to it?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, actually... I'm just sharing it with the janitor.

jokes.text: 'That's stupid. Parties are stupid.' / [pause] / 'I'm stupid. You're shooting a stupid movie.'
jokes.setup: Britta has made a cogent argument about why parties are depressing
jokes.punchline: She then self-destructs, calling everything (including herself) stupid — the escalation of self-criticism is very Britta and lands as a great character beat
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta moment — she makes a good observation, then immediately collapses into self-flagellation. The beats are well-timed (each sentence gets its own moment), and the escalation from 'that's stupid' to 'I'm stupid' is classic Britta self-sabotage. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What is happening here?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My robot is attacking me!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not an attack. It's a malfunction in the programming.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Call the police!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, it's not assaulting her. Look—it's just malfunctioning.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yes! Thank you, Jeff!

jokes.text: 'That's a wrap!' / [crew leaves immediately] / 'Aw!'
jokes.setup: Britta's breakdown inadvertently ends the film
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately calls wrap and the crew disperses — the party-film is over before Britta even understands what happened
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Britta's breakdown as the unexpected dramatic ending to the party-film. Abed's immediate 'That's a wrap' and Britta's 'Aw!' are a good one-two.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I vote yes on the robot purchase.

dialogue.speaker: Robot
dialogue.line: Thank you for your vote. I am now in control.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh no.

jokes.text: 'What's gonna happen to me?' / 'You're going to be punished in ways you won't understand for longer than you think is rational or possible. But then one day, you'll do something he likes, and he'll stop. And eventually you'll either adapt or lose your mind.'
jokes.setup: Willy asks what will happen to him after the program collapses
jokes.punchline: Frankie's clinical description of Jeff's grudge maintenance — 'punished in ways you won't understand for longer than you think is rational' — is both funny and an accurate Jeff character portrait
jokes.explanation: Very good Frankie line — her forensic description of Jeff's petty retribution behavior is both accurate and funny. 'You'll either adapt or lose your mind' is a perfect, dark conclusion. High character integration for Frankie.

jokes.text: Jeff arrives at the ceremony disguised (or sneaking in), gives his speech: 'Dean, I like my job. I don't mind coming to work here. I feel kind of guilty when I pretend to be sick, and I try to steal as little as possible — just the basics. Pens, coffee filters, toilet paper, and one time, an overhead projector and a roll of carpet.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a sincere declaration of affection for the Dean
jokes.punchline: His list of 'stealing as little as possible' escalates from pens to toilet paper to 'an overhead projector and a roll of carpet' — the specificity of the last items makes it very funny
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character monologues. Jeff's 'I try to steal as little as possible' is a perfect Jeff line — damning himself while trying to be sincere. The escalation from pens to 'an overhead projector and a roll of carpet' is beautifully specific. 'The basics' as a category for toilet paper is funny. This is Jeff at his most authentically Jeff.

jokes.text: As a prison warden, I know all too well how rare stories of true rehabilitation can be. But this dean and this prisoner stand here together today to prove that the dream is real.
jokes.setup: The warden gives a moving speech about rehabilitation at the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: The speech is delivered with complete sincerity while we know the actual story — Jeff's manipulation, Willy's attempted murder, the institutional corruption — making every word ironic.
jokes.explanation: Functional ironic framing — the contrast between the speech's idealism and the episode's events is the joke. Not deeply crafted as a standalone line, but serves the scene structure.

jokes.text: Last name? / Geller. / Prisoner ID 042098. / Okay, go on.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to attend the ceremony while on sabbatical from campus, apparently using a robot
jokes.punchline: Jeff giving a prisoner ID number to get onto campus — presumably having logged into the prison system as an inmate to operate a robot — is a funny visual/logical joke about the perverse consequences of the robot program
jokes.explanation: Jeff accessing campus by pretending to be a prisoner using the very program he championed is a satisfying structural callback. The deadpan prison ID exchange is funny because the guard just accepts it. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: Hold it! / Dean, I agree there's no reason you shouldn't give this guy my job...
jokes.setup: Jeff interrupts the ceremony dramatically
jokes.punchline: His dramatic interruption begins with apparent agreement — 'I agree there's no reason you shouldn't give this guy my job' — which is the last thing we'd expect, flipping the convention of the dramatic objection
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the dramatic interruption begins with an unexpected concession. Jeff's willingness to voice his own insecurity is a character note.

jokes.text: 'I'm not just a pretty face that murders people and tells you what you want to hear. I'm less than that. I'm a gorgeous face that works for you and considers you a friend.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is distinguishing himself from Willy (who actually murders people)
jokes.punchline: He corrects himself from 'pretty face that murders people' to 'gorgeous face' — the vanity upgrade in the middle of a sincere speech about not being a murderer is perfect Jeff
